title: Indra and the mirror
hookLine: Indra and a demon king learn the self from a pan of water; atman is not the body
carry: the self is not the body

cards: Another old story. Prajapati, the creator, announced: there is a self that never grows old, never dies, never grieves, never hungers. Whoever finds it wins everything.
Two students came to learn it, firewood in hand, the old sign of a student. Indra, king of the gods. And Virochana, king of the demons.
They served Prajapati for thirty-two years. Then he said: dress in your finest clothes and look into a pan of water. What do you see?
Ourselves, sir, all dressed up, down to our hair and nails. That, said Prajapati, is the self. Both went home happy.

teach.h: VIROCHANA: THE BODY IS THE SELF.
teach.b: Virochana went home and taught the demons: the body is the self. Dress it, feed it, please it, and you win this world and the next.
But Indra, on the road home, stopped. If the body is the self, then when the body is dressed up, the self is dressed up. When the body goes blind, the self goes blind.
When the body dies, the self dies. That's no self that never dies. I see no good in this, he said, and turned around.
Many teachers read Prajapati's answer as a test: the reflection was the easy answer, and only one student questioned it. That's the teaching, and one of Hinduism's biggest: atman, the self.
You have a body, and you are more than it.

teach.h: AYAM ATMA BRAHMA: THIS SELF IS BRAHMAN.
teach.b: The Mandukya's second verse says it plainly: all this is Brahman, and this self is Brahman. Ayam atma brahma, one of the four great sayings, the mahavakyas. Then it maps that self in four quarters.
The first is vaishvanara, the waking self: knowing outward, enjoying solid things, food, faces, the chair under you. In om, it's the first sound, a.
The Mandukya doesn't call waking life fake, or the body bad. Waking is a real quarter. Just not the whole.
Today the pan of water is a phone. A person can spend an hour on one photo and feel their worth rise and fall with it. Hindu teaching doesn't say stop caring how you look.
It says that face is where you live, not who you are. Indra stopped on the road. Anyone can.

how: 'Ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2) is taught in Hindu Vedanta as one of four mahavakyas, great sayings, each drawn from a different Veda.

o: a hymn praising the four great Vedas in order
an Upanishad mapping the self in four quarters
a rule book for the four stages of life

games.q: the pan of water — tap the pairs.

s: Indra was happy with the answer in the pan of water
Virochana was; Indra saw a body-self would go blind and die, and turned back.
the Mandukya says waking life is fake
it says waking is one real quarter of the self, not the whole.
'this self is Brahman' is one of the four great sayings
ayam atma brahma, from the Mandukya.

games.q: you're Indra, walking home. the teacher said the self is your reflection. what bugs you?
o: if the body goes blind or dies, that self would too.
games.why: a body-self would age and die, so it can't be the self that never dies. Indra turned back.

practice: Be fully in the waking state: your weight on the chair, the sounds around you, the air on your skin, the taste in your mouth. This is the first quarter, knowing outward.
Then gently notice that you're aware of all of it, the body included: it's appearing to you. Ask Indra's question quietly, is this all of me, and rest there without answering.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Upanishad. The self is Brahman, and it has four quarters. The first is vaishvanara: the waking state, knowing outward.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vaishvanara, common to all people, universal; the name of the waking self in Mandukya 3.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is not the body. Indra turned back on the road; tomorrow, what Prajapati told him next.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7–8.9.1 (Indra and Virochana; the reflection in the water; Indra turns back)
Mandukya Upanishad 2 (all this is Brahman; this self is Brahman; four quarters)
Shankara, commentary on Mandukya 3 (the nineteen mouths)
